e.t: This word means “peaceable”: it describes a person or conduct characterized by peace rather than conflict. It is an adjective, so it identifies a quality or manner rather than naming an action by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 3:2. Its basic sense is a calm, non-conflicting disposition, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes.

e.t: This word means “recline” or “to recline,” describing the act of leaning or lying back, often taking a resting or seated position. It is an action word rather than the name of a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 11 verses, showing that it describes a recurring physical action in different settings. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what the person is doing when reclining.

This Greek word means “from” or “since.” It points to a starting point, source, or point of separation. Depending on the sentence, it can describe where something comes from, the point from which an action begins, or the time from which something has continued. It is a very common New Testament word, occurring 646 times, so its precise sense is determined by the surrounding words and context. It appears throughout the New Testament, including Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts.

This word refers to greediness—the grasping desire to take what belongs to others—and can also describe plunder, meaning goods seized by force or dishonestly. It therefore points to wrongful taking, whether viewed as an inner craving or as the spoil produced by it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Matthew, Luke, and Hebrews. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Archippus is a personal name referring to a man named in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Colossians and once in Philemon. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself identifies the person, while each passage supplies the further information about him.

e.t: This word means “fearlessly,” describing an action done with courage rather than fear. It functions as an adverb, showing how someone acts or speaks. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its basic sense remains consistent across several passages without being limited to one setting. The surrounding verse determines whether it describes serving, speaking, or another action, but the word itself emphasizes a fearless manner. Its meaning is supported by the word’s lexical definition and its New Testament occurrences.

e.t: This word means “to hurt,” describing the act of causing pain or injury. It functions as a verb, focusing on harm being done to someone rather than merely describing a painful condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing in Mark 16:18 and Luke 4:35. Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the action of hurting or causing harm.

e.t: This word means “eighteen,” the number ten together with eight. It functions as a numeral, identifying a quantity rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 13:4, and the English rendering there is “eighteen.” Its exact significance in that verse comes from the surrounding statement, but the word itself simply names the number eighteen.

This word means “second” or “secondly,” identifying what follows the first in order, sequence, or consideration. It can describe a person or thing that comes next, or mark a subsequent point in a statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 43 times across 42 verses, including passages in the Gospels, Acts, Hebrews, and Revelation. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on whether it describes something second in order or introduces a second point.

e.t: This word means “to keep,” expressing the act of holding on to something, preserving it, or continuing to observe it. It describes deliberate retention rather than simply possessing something for a moment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke and Acts, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding sentence. The word can therefore refer either to maintaining something or faithfully continuing with what has been given or required.

“Double-minded” describes a person whose inner commitment is divided rather than settled in one direction. It points to wavering or inconsistency in thought and purpose, especially when a person is trying to hold two opposing positions at once. This word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in James, where its meaning is expressed through the description “double-minded.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. This word describes something hard to carry—burdensome, heavy, or “ponderous.” It points to a load that is difficult for someone to bear or manage, whether understood as physical weight or as a demanding burden. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains something excessively difficult to carry or bear.

e.t: This word means “to have a custom”: to follow an established or customary practice. It describes something people regularly do as their normal practice, rather than a single isolated action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, showing this word’s use for customary conduct in different settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the practice being described.

e.t: This word means “to run in,” describing someone entering a place by running. It expresses movement into an area with speed or urgency rather than merely being present there. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 12:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains the action of running into a place. Hamor is a personal name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 7:16, and is rendered “Hamor.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a particular person named Hamor rather than expressing a broader idea. The surrounding verse provides the details about that person and his role.

This word means “year” or “years,” referring to a measured period of twelve months or to a period counted by years. It functions as a noun for describing time and may refer to one year or more than one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, including passages in Luke, John, Acts, Hebrews, and Revelation. Its precise significance in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to ring out,” “to ring/sound out,” or “to sound out.” It describes a sound being carried outward so that it can be heard, functioning as a verb rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 1:8. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea is sound spreading outward clearly and audibly.

e.t: This word means “to care for” or “to oversee”—to pay careful attention to people or responsibilities and see that they are properly tended. It describes active, watchful responsibility rather than distant awareness. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews and 1 Peter. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains attentive care and supervision.

e.h: A Word for Snake or Viper
e.t: This word means “snake” or “viper,” referring to a venomous snake. It is a noun used five times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Luke, and Acts. Its ordinary meaning is the animal itself; when used in speech about people, the surrounding passage determines how the image is applied. The word appears in Matthew 3:7, Matthew 12:34, Matthew 23:33, Luke 3:7, and Acts 28:3.

This word means “sight”—something seen or viewed. It refers to the act or experience of looking at something, rather than describing a person, action, or moral quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 23:48, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the word.

This word describes beings as being “like an angel.” It points to resemblance to angels rather than identifying the beings as angels themselves. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 20:36. Its central meaning is therefore a comparison: the beings share an angel-like quality or condition. The exact significance of that comparison in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself expresses likeness to an angel.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to harm”—to injure, damage, or treat someone in a harmful way. It functions as a verb, describing an action directed against another person or group. It occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, appearing five times in Acts and once in 1 Peter. The word’s basic sense remains focused on causing harm, whether through hostile treatment or damaging action. The surrounding verse determines the specific kind of harm intended in each occurrence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to fall down.” It describes movement from a higher position to a lower one, or the act of collapsing downward. Its basic sense is physical and directional, though the surrounding verse determines precisely how the action is understood. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Acts. Its appearances include Luke 8:6, Acts 26:14, and Acts 28:6, but the individual verse contexts must supply the specific force of the action.

This word means “respectable,” describing someone or something worthy of proper regard. It functions as an adjective, so it characterizes a person or conduct rather than naming an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, both in 1 Timothy. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains what is fitting to respect and regard honorably.

This word means “harbor,” referring to a sheltered place where ships can anchor or find protection from open water. It is a noun describing a physical maritime location, not an action or personal quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts 27, where the discussion concerns places suitable for a ship to remain. Its precise significance in any one occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means a bucket or large bowl, referring to a sizable container used to hold something. It is a noun describing an ordinary household vessel rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its appearances belong to sayings that use the familiar image of a container, but the precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage. The central idea remains a substantial vessel that can be placed over or beneath something.

e.t: This word means “be sick” or “to be unhealthy.” It describes a person whose condition is marked by illness or poor health, rather than expressing a healthy state. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:4. Its basic sense is physical or figurative weakness, while the surrounding verse determines how that condition is being applied. The word itself centers on being unwell or lacking health.

e.t: This word means “to anger” or “to be angry.” It describes the experience or expression of anger, and it functions as a verb—that is, it presents anger as something a person does or comes to feel. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, showing repeated use for people who become angry or act from anger. The surrounding passage determines who is angry and what prompted that anger; the word itself identifies the emotional response rather than explaining every circumstance. Its New Testament usage extends from Matthew through Revelation.

This word refers to a stranger or temporary resident—someone living in a place that is not their permanent home. It describes a person who belongs elsewhere and therefore lives as a visitor or sojourner among others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Hebrews and twice in 1 Peter. Its basic sense points to a limited earthly residence and a person whose true home lies beyond the place where they presently live.

It describes something increasing greatly, existing in plentiful supply, or going beyond a measure or standard. Depending on the sentence, it may refer to material abundance, overflowing actions or qualities, or surpassing what is required. It occurs 39 times in the Greek New Testament, showing a broad use centered on having more than enough or going beyond the expected amount.

e.t: This word means to sail, travel by ship, or move across the water in a vessel. It describes seafaring movement rather than travel by land, and it can refer either to the act of sailing or to people and vessels making such a journey. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including accounts of journeys in Luke and Acts and a reference involving ships in Revelation. Its exact wording in English may appear as “sailed” or “sail,” but the central idea remains travel by sea.

This word means “purple,” describing a rich, distinctive color. In the New Testament, it is used for clothing or material connected with scenes of honor, luxury, or display, though the precise significance depends on the surrounding passage. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament: twice in John and twice in Revelation. It consistently identifies the color itself rather than expressing an action or abstract idea.

Samaria is the name of a region in the land of Israel. In the New Testament, the word identifies the place and its inhabitants or things associated with it, depending on the sentence. It appears 11 times in the Greek New Testament, especially in Acts and John. The name is connected with locations Jesus and his followers encountered and with the spread of witness beyond Jerusalem. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word expresses dying with someone or being destroyed with someone or something. Its meanings include “to destroy with” and “to die with,” describing an action connected to another person or thing rather than an isolated death or destruction. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at Hebrews 11:31. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding sentence, but the word itself centers on sharing death or destruction with another.

Sosthenes is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, once in Acts and once in 1 Corinthians. The English Bible preserves it as “Sosthenes,” so the word functions as a name identifying an individual. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish additional details about his character, role, or relationship to others.

e.t: This word means to bring something to its end or completion. It can describe an action that is being carried out, has been completed, or has reached its intended result. Its glosses include “by performing,” “finished,” “had finished,” “to finish,” and “were finished.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, so its precise force depends on what action or purpose the surrounding sentence presents.

This word means “manner” or “way,” describing how something happens or the way a person or thing is understood. It can point to a method, pattern, or manner of conduct, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, so its central idea is consistent while its precise sense is shaped by context. The word appears in passages from Matthew, Luke, Acts, Paul’s letters, Hebrews, and Jude.

This word means an “upper room” or “upstairs room”—a room located on an upper level of a building. It is a place-name word, describing the room itself rather than an action, feeling, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Acts, where it identifies a particular kind of room. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is simply a room above the main level of a house or building.

Perishable describes something that does not last permanently but can decay, spoil, or pass away. It points to a temporary condition rather than something enduring. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs six times, including passages that contrast perishable things with what is lasting. Its basic sense remains focused on vulnerability to decline or disappearance, while the surrounding verse determines what particular thing is being described.

e.t: This word means “Canaanite,” identifying a person as belonging to the Canaanite people. It functions as a descriptive name for ethnic or national identity rather than expressing an action, quality, or emotion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 15:22. The word itself identifies Canaanite heritage; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s particular circumstances or the significance of the reference there.

This word refers to a woman whose husband has died—a widow. It identifies her as a particular social and family circumstance, whether the word appears in the singular or plural. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times and is used in passages referring to widows in need, widows receiving care, and widows acting with persistent appeal. Its central meaning remains the person herself: a woman living without her deceased husband.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to delineate” or “to write.” It describes the act of marking something out, recording it, or putting words down in writing. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at John 8:6. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its exact action in that occurrence cannot be stated more narrowly. Its basic sense remains an intentional act of setting something down or defining it in written form.
